name: The Italian Game
blurb: The oldest opening still played at every level: bishop to c4, pointed at f7.

steps.note: 1.e4. The move takes the centre and opens two pieces at once — the bishop on f1 and the queen. Almost everything in this lesson follows from the bishop's diagonal being open on move one.

1...e5 is the classical reply: Black stakes the same claim and refuses to give White a free centre. It is also the move that concedes the most, because the pawn on e5 needs defending and the knight on b8 is the piece that has to do it.
2.Nf3 develops with a threat. There is exactly one thing to say about this move and it is the whole of White's early play: it attacks e5, so Black's reply is not free.

2...Nc6 defends the pawn and develops. Note what Black has *not* done: 2...d6 also defends e5, but it shuts in the dark-squared bishop. Defending with a piece rather than a pawn is the better habit when both are available.

3.Bc4 is the Italian Game. The bishop takes the a2–g8 diagonal, and the square it is really looking at is f7 — the one square in Black's camp defended by the king alone. This is not a threat yet. It is a bishop placed where threats become available later.
3...Bc5 is the Giuoco Piano — "the quiet game". Black mirrors the idea exactly, pointing a bishop at f2. The position is symmetrical and the fight is about who gets to break it first.

4.c3 is the point of the whole system. It prepares d4, which is the move that hits the bishop on c5 and claims the centre in one go. The cost is that the b1 knight has lost its natural square, and White accepts that for the pawn break.
4...Nf6 develops and hits e4. Black is not waiting to be told what the plan is — the knight attacks something, so White has to spend the next move dealing with it.

5.d3 is the modern choice, and the resulting position is called the Giuoco Pianissimo — the very quiet game. White defends e4, gives up on an immediate d4, and plans a slow build with Nbd2, Bb3 and a later d4 once the pieces are ready. It looks tame. It is the most common way strong players handle this position, because the alternative — 5.d4 straight away — gives Black concrete play immediately.
Back to move three, and a different reply. 3...Nf6 is the Two Knights Defence, and it changes the character completely: instead of mirroring, Black attacks e4 at once and invites a fight.

4.Ng5 is the move that makes this variation famous, and it breaks a rule you were probably taught — do not move the same piece twice in the opening. It is justified by one thing only: it attacks f7 twice, with the knight and the bishop, and f7 is defended once.

4...d5 is the only good answer, and it is a counter-attack rather than a defence. Black does not defend f7 at all — instead the pawn blocks the bishop's diagonal, which is what was making the threat work.

5.exd5. White takes, and now the natural-looking recapture 5...Nxd5 runs into 6.Nxf7, which is a real sacrifice with a long theoretical history. This is the moment the Two Knights stops being a normal opening.

5...Na5 is the main line, and it is worth understanding why a move that puts a knight on the rim is correct here. It attacks the bishop on c4 — the piece that makes every threat against f7 work — and forces it to move before White can organise anything. Black gives up a pawn for the time to develop. If you play the Italian as White, this is the position you need an answer to.
